title: La cuenta dividida en el café de Madrid

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Pablo, el camarero dice que no nos divide la cuenta en la terraza.
dialogue.english: Hey, Pablo, the waiter says he won't split the bill for us on the patio.

dialogue.speaker: Pablo
dialogue.spanish: ¡Qué fuerte! Bueno, no pasa nada, pago yo todo con tarjeta porque andas sin pasta.
dialogue.english: That's wild! Well, no worries, I'll pay the whole thing by card since you're out of cash.

slang.actualMeaning: money / cash (very common slang across Spain)
slang.example: No salgo este finde porque no tengo nada de pasta.

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.spanish: Mil gracias, tío. Te hago un Bizum de doce euros ahora mismo por mis tostadas y el cortado.
dialogue.english: Thanks a million, dude. I'll send you a 12-euro Bizum transfer right now for my toast and espresso.

slang.actualMeaning: dude / mate / guy (everyday Spanish friend address)
slang.example: ¡Gracias por esperarme, tío!

dialogue.speaker: Pablo
dialogue.spanish: Vale, genial. Vámonos pitando que el metro cierra en veinte minutos.
dialogue.english: Okay, great. Let's get out of here fast because the metro closes in twenty minutes.

slang.actualMeaning: in a big hurry / right away (irse pitando)
slang.example: Salí pitando de la oficina para no perder el tren.

questions.question: What problem do Carmen and Pablo run into at the Madrid café?
options: The waiter says he won't split the bill on the patio
The credit card machine is broken
The kitchen ran out of toast and coffee
They forgot their phones at home
questions.explanation: Carmen says: 'el camarero dice que no nos divide la cuenta en la terraza' (the waiter won't split the bill).

questions.question: How does Carmen pay Pablo back for her share?
options: She gives him a 20-euro bill in cash
She sends him a 12-euro Bizum mobile transfer
She buys his metro ticket at the station
She promises to buy breakfast tomorrow
questions.explanation: Carmen says: 'Te hago un Bizum de doce euros ahora mismo por mis tostadas y el cortado.'

questions.question: Why do they need to leave the café quickly at the end?
options: It is starting to rain on the patio
The metro closes in 20 minutes
They have a movie reservation at eight
The café is closing its terrace
questions.explanation: Pablo says: 'Vámonos pitando que el metro cierra en veinte minutos.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: When Pablo says 'andas sin pasta' and 'vámonos pitando', what do 'pasta' and 'irse pitando' mean in Spain?
options: 'Pasta' = money/cash; 'irse pitando' = to leave in a hurry
'Pasta' = Italian food; 'irse pitando' = to whistle a song
'Pasta' = patience; 'irse pitando' = to take a taxi
'Pasta' = battery; 'irse pitando' = to argue with the waiter
questions.explanation: In Spain, 'pasta' is slang for money/cash, and 'irse pitando' means to leave in a rush!

dialogue.speaker: Julieta
dialogue.spanish: Che, Tomás, la línea D del subte está cortada por obras. ¿Cómo vamos al centro?
dialogue.english: Hey, Tomás, subway Line D is closed for maintenance. How do we get downtown?

slang.actualMeaning: the Buenos Aires subway / metro system
slang.example: Tomamos el subte en Plaza Italia para llegar rápido.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.spanish: ¡Qué garrón! Encima no tengo saldo en la tarjeta SUBE para tomar el colectivo.
dialogue.english: What a bummer! On top of that, I don't have balance on my SUBE transit card to take the bus.

slang.actualMeaning: a total bummer / drag / bad luck (Argentine slang)
slang.example: ¡Qué garrón que se largó a llover justo ahora!

dialogue.speaker: Julieta
dialogue.spanish: Tranquilo, boludo, acá a media cuadra hay un kiosco donde cargan la tarjeta.
dialogue.english: Relax, dude, half a block from here there's a convenience stand where they top up the card.

slang.actualMeaning: dude / buddy (friendly everyday Argentine address between friends)
slang.example: Che, boludo, ¿a qué hora nos vemos hoy?

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.spanish: Bárbaro. Carguemos mil pesos y paso a comprar unas medialunas para el viaje.
dialogue.english: Awesome. Let's load a thousand pesos and I'll stop to buy some croissants for the ride.

questions.question: Why can't Julieta and Tomás take the subway ('el subte') downtown?
options: Line D is closed due to maintenance work
They lost their SUBE transit cards
The station already closed for the night
The train is too crowded to board
questions.explanation: Julieta explains: 'la línea D del subte está cortada por obras' (Line D is closed for maintenance work).

questions.question: Where do they go to add balance to Tomás's SUBE transit card?
options: A bank two blocks away
A neighborhood kiosk ('un kiosco') half a block away
A supermarket across the avenue
They pay the bus driver in coins
questions.explanation: Julieta says: 'acá a media cuadra hay un kiosco donde cargan la tarjeta.'

questions.question: How much money does Tomás want to load, and what snack does he mention?
options: 500 pesos and empanadas
1,000 pesos and croissants ('medialunas')
2,000 pesos and a coffee
300 pesos and a sandwich
questions.explanation: Tomás says: 'Carguemos mil pesos y paso a comprar unas medialunas para el viaje.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: When Tomás exclaims '¡Qué garrón!', what does 'un garrón' mean in Argentine Spanish?
options: A total bummer / drag / piece of bad luck
A great bargain / discount
A fast express train
A delicious bakery pastry
questions.explanation: In Argentina, '¡Qué garrón!' means 'What a bummer!' or 'What a drag!'

title: Fruta fresca en la plaza de Medellín

dialogue.speaker: Camila
dialogue.spanish: ¡Quiubo, parcero! Mirá qué lulos tan bonitos tienen en este puesto de la plaza.
dialogue.english: What's up, buddy! Look how nice the lulo fruits are at this market stall.

slang.actualMeaning: buddy / close friend (iconic Colombian slang)
slang.example: Ese man es mi parcero desde el colegio.

dialogue.speaker: Sebastián
dialogue.spanish: ¡Están una chimba! Llevemos una bolsa para hacer jugo frío en la casa.
dialogue.english: They look amazing! Let's get a bag to make cold juice at home.

slang.actualMeaning: fantastic / amazing / top-notch (Medellín slang)
slang.example: ¡El concierto de anoche estuvo una chimba!

dialogue.speaker: Camila
dialogue.spanish: La señora dice que la docena vale ocho mil pesos y nos regala dos maracuyás de ñapa.
dialogue.english: The lady says a dozen costs eight thousand pesos and she'll throw in two passion fruits as a free bonus.

slang.actualMeaning: as a free extra / baker's dozen bonus at a market
slang.example: Compré tres empanadas y me dieron una más de ñapa.

dialogue.speaker: Sebastián
dialogue.spanish: ¡De una! Pagá vos en efectivo que yo te invito las arepas de queso ahorita.
dialogue.english: Let's do it! You pay in cash and I'll treat you to cheese corn cakes right now.

questions.question: Why do Camila and Sebastián want to buy 'lulos' at the Medellín market?
options: To make cold juice at home
To bake a birthday cake
To bring them to their office party
To sell them at their own restaurant
questions.explanation: Sebastián says: 'Llevemos una bolsa para hacer jugo frío en la casa.'

questions.question: How much does a dozen cost, and what does the vendor include for free?
options: 5,000 pesos plus free bananas
8,000 pesos plus two free passion fruits ('dos maracuyás de ñapa')
10,000 pesos plus a glass of orange juice
12,000 pesos plus a cheese arepa
questions.explanation: Camila says: 'la docena vale ocho mil pesos y nos regala dos maracuyás de ñapa.'

questions.question: What does Sebastián offer to buy for Camila if she pays cash at the fruit stand?
options: Cheese corn cakes ('arepas de queso')
Two cups of Colombian coffee
A taxi ride home
Tickets to a soccer match
questions.explanation: Sebastián says: 'Pagá vos en efectivo que yo te invito las arepas de queso ahorita.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Colombian Spanish, what do 'parcero', 'una chimba', and 'de ñapa' mean?
options: 'Parcero' = friend/buddy; 'una chimba' = amazing/cool; 'de ñapa' = as a free bonus
'Parcero' = vendor; 'una chimba' = expensive; 'de ñapa' = on credit
'Parcero' = cousin; 'una chimba' = sour; 'de ñapa' = tomorrow
'Parcero' = neighbor; 'una chimba' = heavy; 'de ñapa' = in a bag
questions.explanation: In Colombia, 'parcero' means friend/buddy, 'una chimba' means awesome/amazing, and 'de ñapa' is a free extra thrown in by a vendor!

title: Tacos de canasta afuera del metro

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Valeria, tengo muchísima hambre. ¿Vamos por unos tacos de canasta aquí afuera del metro?
dialogue.english: Hey, Valeria, I'm super hungry. Shall we get some basket tacos right outside the subway?

slang.actualMeaning: Steamed street tacos kept warm in a cloth-lined basket, often sold from a bicycle
slang.example: En la esquina del metro venden tacos de canasta buenísimos.

dialogue.speaker: Valeria
dialogue.spanish: ¡Ay, sí, qué rico! Pero espera, ¿tienes efectivo? Es que el señor de la bicicleta no acepta tarjeta.
dialogue.english: Oh, yes, delicious! But wait, do you have cash? The guy with the bicycle doesn't take cards.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.spanish: Híjole, solo traigo un billete de cincuenta pesos. ¿Cuánto cuestan?
dialogue.english: Shoot, I only have a fifty-peso bill on me. How much do they cost?

slang.actualMeaning: Shoot! / Gosh! / Oh man! (mild Mexican exclamation of surprise)
slang.example: ¡Híjole, se me olvidaron las llaves adentro de la casa!

dialogue.speaker: Valeria
dialogue.spanish: La orden de cinco tacos cuesta cuarenta pesos. Y yo traigo veinte pesos en monedas para dos refrescos.
dialogue.english: An order of five tacos costs forty pesos. And I have twenty pesos in coins for two sodas.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.spanish: ¡Ah, qué chido! Entonces compartimos la orden ahorita y luego en la tarde te pago con transferencia.
dialogue.english: Oh, awesome! Then let's share the order right now and later this afternoon I'll pay you back by bank transfer.

slang.actualMeaning: How awesome / great / cool (classic Mexican slang)
slang.example: ¡Qué chido que pudiste venir a la fiesta!

dialogue.speaker: Valeria
dialogue.spanish: Sale, pide dos de papa con chorizo y tres de frijol. ¡Pero cuidado con la salsa verde que pica un montón!
dialogue.english: Deal, order two potato-and-chorizo ones and three bean ones. But watch out for the green salsa—it's super spicy!

slang.actualMeaning: It's super spicy / has a lot of chili heat
slang.example: No le pongas tanta salsa habanera porque pica un montón.

questions.question: What are Carlos and Valeria trying to figure out outside the subway station ('afuera del metro')?
options: Whether they have enough cash ('efectivo') to buy street tacos and sodas ('refrescos')
Which subway line ('línea del metro') they need to take to get to a restaurant
Where to find an ATM ('cajero') because they lost their wallets
How to cook potato and bean tacos ('tacos de papa y frijol') at home tonight
questions.explanation: Carlos is hungry for tacos de canasta outside the metro, and Valeria checks if they have enough cash ('efectivo') since the bicycle vendor doesn't take cards.

questions.question: How much money does Carlos have on him, and how much does an order of 5 tacos cost?
options: He has a 20-peso bill ('veinte pesos'), and the tacos cost 50 pesos ('cincuenta pesos')
He has a 50-peso bill ('cincuenta pesos'), and the 5 tacos cost 40 pesos ('cuarenta pesos')
He has 100 pesos in coins ('cien pesos'), and the tacos cost 60 pesos ('sesenta pesos')
He has no cash at all, so Valeria pays 40 pesos by card ('con tarjeta')
questions.explanation: Carlos says 'solo traigo un billete de cincuenta pesos' (50-peso bill), and Valeria says 'La orden de cinco tacos cuesta cuarenta pesos' (40 pesos).

questions.question: Which taco fillings does Valeria ask Carlos to order for them to share?
options: Five pork tacos with red salsa ('cinco de carnitas con salsa roja')
Three chicken tacos and two cheese tacos ('tres de pollo y dos de queso')
Two potato-with-chorizo and three bean tacos ('dos de papa con chorizo y tres de frijol')
Four steak tacos and one potato taco ('cuatro de bistec y uno de papa')
questions.explanation: Valeria says: 'Sale, pide dos de papa con chorizo y tres de frijol' (two potato-with-chorizo and three bean tacos).

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: When Carlos says 'Híjole', '¡qué chido!', and Valeria warns that the salsa 'pica un montón', what do those expressions mean?
options: 'Híjole' = shoot/oh man; 'qué chido' = how awesome; 'pica un montón' = it's super spicy
'Híjole' = hurry up; 'qué chido' = how expensive; 'pica un montón' = it costs extra
'Híjole' = excuse me; 'qué chido' = how cold; 'pica un montón' = it's sour
'Híjole' = thank you; 'qué chido' = how small; 'pica un montón' = it's very hot
questions.explanation: In Mexican Spanish, 'híjole' is 'shoot/oh man', 'qué chido' is 'how cool/awesome', and 'pica un montón' means 'it's super spicy!'

title: El café de olla y el pan dulce en Coyoacán

dialogue.speaker: Sofía
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Luis, ¿pedimos dos cafés de olla aquí en la panadería antes de tomar el camión?
dialogue.english: Hey, Luis, should we order two spiced pot coffees here at the bakery before taking the bus?

slang.actualMeaning: city passenger bus (standard everyday word in Mexico)
slang.example: El camión al centro pasa cada diez minutos.

dialogue.speaker: Luis
dialogue.spanish: ¿Mande? Perdón, estaba viendo mi celular. Sí, buena idea, hace bastante frío esta mañana.
dialogue.english: Pardon? Sorry, I was looking at my phone. Yes, good idea, it's pretty cold this morning.

slang.actualMeaning: Pardon? / What did you say? (Polite Mexican way to ask someone to repeat)
slang.example: ¿Mande, abuelita? No te escuché bien.

dialogue.speaker: Sofía
dialogue.spanish: También voy a llevar dos conchas de vainilla para desayunar en la oficina. Son treinta y cinco pesos en total.
dialogue.english: I'm also going to get two vanilla sweet breads to eat for breakfast at the office. It's thirty-five pesos total.

dialogue.speaker: Luis
dialogue.spanish: Yo invito hoy, Sofía. Pero apúrate porque nuestro camión pasa en ocho minutos por la avenida.
dialogue.english: It's my treat today, Sofía. But hurry up because our bus comes down the avenue in eight minutes.

slang.actualMeaning: It's my treat / I'm paying for both of us
slang.example: Guarda tu cartera, hoy yo invito los tacos.

questions.question: Why does Luis say '¿Mande?' when Sofía first speaks to him?
options: He was looking at his phone and didn't catch what she said
He doesn't like spiced coffee
He forgot his wallet at home
The bakery music is too loud
questions.explanation: Luis replies: '¿Mande? Perdón, estaba viendo mi celular.'

questions.question: What does Sofía pick up to eat at the office, and how much is the total?
options: Two vanilla conchas (sweet breads) for 35 pesos total
Three churros for 50 pesos total
One ham sandwich for 45 pesos total
Two tamales for 30 pesos total
questions.explanation: Sofía gets 'dos conchas de vainilla para desayunar en la oficina. Son treinta y cinco pesos en total.'

questions.question: Why does Luis tell Sofía to hurry up at the end?
options: Their bus ('el camión') comes down the avenue in 8 minutes
The bakery is about to close
It is starting to rain outside
Their boss just called on his cell phone
questions.explanation: Luis says: 'apúrate porque nuestro camión pasa en ocho minutos por la avenida.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Mexican Spanish, what do '¿Mande?', 'el camión', and 'Yo invito' mean?
options: '¿Mande?' = Pardon?; 'el camión' = the city bus; 'Yo invito' = It's my treat
'¿Mande?' = Send it; 'el camión' = the subway; 'Yo invito' = Come to my party
'¿Mande?' = Hurry up; 'el camión' = the bicycle; 'Yo invito' = Let's split it
'¿Mande?' = Excuse me; 'el camión' = the taxi; 'Yo invito' = You pay today
questions.explanation: In Mexico, '¿Mande?' is the polite way to say 'Pardon?', 'el camión' is the passenger bus, and 'Yo invito' means 'My treat!'

title: Tapas de última hora en Lavapiés

dialogue.speaker: Lucía
dialogue.spanish: ¡Hola, Javi! ¿Qué tal el curro hoy? Te veo con una cara de cansado impresionante.
dialogue.english: Hi, Javi! How was work today? You look completely exhausted.

slang.actualMeaning: work / job (everyday colloquial word in Spain)
slang.example: Salgo del curro a las seis y nos vemos en el centro.

dialogue.speaker: Javi
dialogue.spanish: Uf, ni me hables, tía. Estuve liado con un informe toda la tarde, pero ya tengo hambre.
dialogue.english: Phew, don't even get me started, girl. I was tied up with a report all afternoon, but now I'm hungry.

slang.actualMeaning: swamped / super busy with something
slang.example: Perdona que no te llamara, anduve muy liado toda la mañana.

dialogue.speaker: Lucía
dialogue.spanish: Venga, entremos a esta taberna que ponen unas patatas bravas que flipas por cinco euros.
dialogue.english: Come on, let's go into this tavern—they serve mind-blowing patatas bravas for five euros.

slang.actualMeaning: mind-blowing / incredible / amazing (Spain slang)
slang.example: Hicieron una paella que flipas.

dialogue.speaker: Javi
dialogue.spanish: ¡De lujo! Pide tú dos cañas bien frías mientras busco una mesa libre al fondo.
dialogue.english: Awesome! You order two ice-cold draft beers while I look for an empty table in the back.

slang.actualMeaning: two small glasses of draft beer (standard across Spain)
slang.example: Nos tomamos dos cañas con unas aceitunas en la plaza.

questions.question: Why does Javi look so tired when he meets Lucía?
options: He was swamped working on a report all afternoon
He walked all the way across Madrid in the rain
He stayed up late watching a soccer match
He just came back from the gym
questions.explanation: Javi explains: 'Estuve liado con un informe toda la tarde' (he was swamped with a report all afternoon).

questions.question: What food does Lucía recommend at the tavern, and how much does it cost?
options: Patatas bravas for 5 euros
Spanish tortilla for 10 euros
Calamari sandwiches for 8 euros
Ham croquettes for 12 euros
questions.explanation: Lucía says: 'ponen unas patatas bravas que flipas por cinco euros.'

questions.question: What does Javi ask Lucía to order while he looks for a table in the back?
options: Two cold draft beers ('dos cañas bien frías')
A pitcher of sangria
Two bottles of sparkling water
Two cups of espresso
questions.explanation: Javi says: 'Pide tú dos cañas bien frías mientras busco una mesa libre al fondo.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Spain, what do 'el curro', 'estar liado', and 'que flipas' mean?
options: 'El curro' = work/job; 'estar liado' = to be swamped/busy; 'que flipas' = mind-blowing/amazing
'El curro' = the bus; 'estar liado' = to be lost; 'que flipas' = overpriced
'El curro' = the boss; 'estar liado' = to be hungry; 'que flipas' = very spicy
'El curro' = the gym; 'estar liado' = to be sleepy; 'que flipas' = frozen
questions.explanation: In Spain, 'el curro' means work, 'estar liado' means to be busy/swamped, and 'que flipas' means amazing/mind-blowing!

title: Asado del domingo en San Telmo

dialogue.speaker: Martín
dialogue.spanish: Che, Flor, acá en la carnicería del mercado queda el último kilo de vacío para el asado.
dialogue.english: Hey, Flor, right here at the market butcher shop they have the last kilo of flank steak for the barbecue.

dialogue.speaker: Flor
dialogue.spanish: ¡Qué joya! Llevate también cuatro chorizos y una bolsa de carbón antes de que se acabe.
dialogue.english: What a gem! Grab four sausages and a bag of charcoal too before it sells out.

slang.actualMeaning: awesome / fantastic / great news (Argentine slang)
slang.example: ¿Conseguiste entradas para el partido? ¡Joya!

dialogue.speaker: Martín
dialogue.spanish: Dale, son doce mil mangos en total. ¿Ponemos mitad y mitad o pagás vos las bebidas?
dialogue.english: Sounds good, it's twelve thousand pesos total. Should we split it fifty-fifty or do you want to buy the drinks?

slang.actualMeaning: bucks / pesos (classic Argentine slang for money)
slang.example: Esta campera me salió veinte mil mangos.

dialogue.speaker: Flor
dialogue.spanish: Yo compro el vino tinto y el pan acá al lado. ¡Nos va a quedar re copado el almuerzo!
dialogue.english: I'll buy the red wine and bread right next door. Lunch is going to turn out super cool!

slang.actualMeaning: super cool / awesome (Argentine 're' + 'copado')
slang.example: El lugar nuevo en Palermo está re copado.

questions.question: What items do Martín and Flor buy at the butcher shop for Sunday's barbecue?
options: The last kilo of 'vacío' (flank steak), four sausages ('chorizos'), and charcoal
Two chickens, potatoes, and salad greens
Fish fillets, lemons, and white wine
Pork ribs and a dozen empanadas
questions.explanation: Martín spots 'el último kilo de vacío' and Flor tells him: 'Llevate también cuatro chorizos y una bolsa de carbón.'

questions.question: How much does the butcher shop order cost in total?
options: 5,000 pesos
8,000 pesos
12,000 pesos ('doce mil mangos')
20,000 pesos
questions.explanation: Martín says: 'Dale, son doce mil mangos en total' (12,000 pesos total).

questions.question: How do they divide the expenses for the barbecue?
options: Martín pays for the meat/charcoal, and Flor buys the red wine and bread next door
Flor pays for everything with her credit card
They ask their friends to transfer money first
They decide to eat at a restaurant instead
questions.explanation: Flor says: 'Yo compro el vino tinto y el pan acá al lado.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Argentina, what do 'doce mil mangos' and 're copado' mean?
options: 'Mangos' = pesos/bucks; 're copado' = super cool / awesome
'Mangos' = tropical fruit; 're copado' = way too crowded
'Mangos' = coins; 're copado' = burnt on the grill
'Mangos' = grams; 're copado' = very expensive
questions.explanation: In Argentine Spanish, 'mangos' means pesos/bucks, and 're copado' means super cool or awesome!

title: Un tinto antes del aguacero en Bogotá

dialogue.speaker: Natalia
dialogue.spanish: Uy, Andrés, mirá esas nubes negras sobre los cerros. Se va a venir un aguacero tenaz.
dialogue.english: Whoa, Andrés, look at those dark clouds over the hills. A fierce downpour is about to hit.

slang.actualMeaning: intense / fierce / crazy (very common Bogotá slang)
slang.example: El tráfico por la Séptima hoy está tenaz.

dialogue.speaker: Andrés
dialogue.spanish: Sí, qué frío tan berraco. Entremos a esta cafetería y nos tomamos un tinto bien caliente.
dialogue.english: Yeah, it's freezing cold. Let's duck into this café and have a piping hot black coffee.

slang.actualMeaning: a cup of black coffee (in Colombia, 'tinto' means black coffee, not red wine!)
slang.example: ¿Me regala un tinto sin azúcar, por favor?

dialogue.speaker: Natalia
dialogue.spanish: Buena idea. Y pidamos dos almojábanas recién salidas del horno mientras escampa.
dialogue.english: Good idea. And let's order two cheese breads fresh out of the oven while the rain lets up.

dialogue.speaker: Andrés
dialogue.spanish: Listo, de una. Apenas pare la lluvia caminamos a la estación de TransMilenio.
dialogue.english: Done, let's do it. As soon as the rain stops we'll walk to the TransMilenio bus station.

slang.actualMeaning: right away / let's do it / count me in
slang.example: ¿Vamos a almorzar ya? ¡De una!

questions.question: Why do Natalia and Andrés decide to duck into a café in Bogotá?
options: It's freezing cold and a heavy rainstorm ('aguacero') is about to start
They have a business meeting with a client there
Andrés needs Wi-Fi to send an email
The TransMilenio station is closed
questions.explanation: Natalia sees dark clouds ('se va a venir un aguacero tenaz') and Andrés says it's freezing cold ('qué frío tan berraco').

questions.question: What food do they order to go with their hot drinks?
options: Two warm cheese breads ('almojábanas') fresh from the oven
Two slices of chocolate cake
A plate of fried plantains
Two beef empanadas
questions.explanation: Natalia says: 'Y pidamos dos almojábanas recién salidas del horno mientras escampa.'

questions.question: What is their plan once the rain stops ('mientras escampa')?
options: Walk to the TransMilenio bus station
Call a taxi to go to the airport
Visit a museum downtown
Go grocery shopping
questions.explanation: Andrés says: 'Apenas pare la lluvia caminamos a la estación de TransMilenio.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: When Andrés orders 'un tinto bien caliente' in Colombia, what is he ordering?
options: A cup of hot black coffee (not red wine!)
A glass of mulled red wine
A cup of hot chocolate with cheese
A herbal tea with honey
questions.explanation: False-friend alert! In Colombia, 'un tinto' always means a small cup of black coffee, whereas in Spain 'vino tinto' is red wine.

title: El coche prestado y el raspón en Guadalajara

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Fernanda, no manches... Acabo de bajar al estacionamiento y vi que mi coche tiene un raspón enorme en la defensa trasera.
dialogue.english: Hey, Fernanda, no way... I just went down to the parking lot and saw that my car has a huge scratch on the back bumper.

slang.actualMeaning: No way! / You've got to be kidding me!
slang.example: ¡No manches, qué rápido llegaste!

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: Ay, Diego, te iba a decir ahorita que saliéramos. Ayer que me lo prestaste para ir por las cosas de mi chamba, un poste estaba súper pegado en la rampa.
dialogue.english: Oh, Diego, I was going to tell you right now when we went out. Yesterday when you lent it to me to pick up my work stuff, a pillar was super close on the ramp.

slang.actualMeaning: work / job (everyday Mexican slang)
slang.example: Conseguí una nueva chamba cerca de mi casa.

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: ¿Y pensabas hacerte pato o qué? Sabes que lo acabo de sacar del taller hace dos semanas.
dialogue.english: And were you planning to play dumb or what? You know I just got it out of the repair shop two weeks ago.

slang.actualMeaning: to play dumb / dodge responsibility
slang.example: No te hagas pato, te toca lavar los platos.

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: ¡Claro que no me iba a hacer pato! Ya hablé con el taller de mi tío Memo en Zapopan. Dice que mañana mismo lo pule y lo pinta por mil quinientos pesos.
dialogue.english: Of course I wasn't going to play dumb! I already spoke with my uncle Memo's body shop in Zapopan. He says tomorrow he'll buff and paint it for fifteen hundred pesos.

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: Bueno, menos mal... Pero esa lana la pones tú, ¿eh? Y me llevas a mi oficina en la mañana mientras lo arreglan.
dialogue.english: Well, thank goodness... But you're paying that cash, alright? And you're driving me to my office in the morning while they fix it.

slang.actualMeaning: money / cash (Mexican slang)
slang.example: Ahorré una buena lana para las vacaciones.

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: Trato hecho. Yo pago todo el taller y encima te compro tu torta ahogada para que se te baje el coraje.
dialogue.english: Deal. I'll pay for the whole shop and on top of that I'll buy you your drowned pork sandwich so you stop being mad.

questions.question: Why is Diego upset with Fernanda at the start of the conversation?
options: He found a big scratch on the back bumper of his car after lending it to her
She returned his car with an empty gas tank
She forgot to pick him up from the repair shop
She parked his car in a tow-away zone
questions.explanation: Diego saw a huge scratch ('un raspón enorme') on the rear bumper ('la defensa trasera') after lending his car to Fernanda yesterday.

questions.question: How did the car get scratched, and what plan did Fernanda already arrange?
options: She scraped a tight pillar on a ramp; her Uncle Memo's shop in Zapopan will buff and paint it tomorrow for 1,500 pesos
Another driver hit her in traffic; her insurance will pay 3,000 pesos
A shopping cart hit the door; she bought touch-up paint for 500 pesos
She backed into a tree; Diego's mechanic will fix it next week
questions.explanation: Fernanda scraped a tight pillar on a ramp and arranged for her Uncle Memo's body shop in Zapopan to buff and paint it tomorrow for 1,500 pesos.

questions.question: In addition to Fernanda paying for the repair, what else does Diego demand—and what food does Fernanda offer him?
options: She must drive him to his office in the morning, and she offers to buy him a 'torta ahogada'
She must wash his car, and she offers him street tacos
She must lend him her bicycle, and she offers to buy him coffee
She must pay his parking fee, and she offers to cook dinner
questions.explanation: Diego insists she pay the cash ('esa lana la pones tú') and drive him to his office in the morning, and she offers him a 'torta ahogada'.

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: What do the Mexican idioms 'hacerse pato', 'la chamba', and 'la lana' mean?
options: 'Hacerse pato' = play dumb; 'la chamba' = work/job; 'la lana' = money/cash
'Hacerse pato' = drive fast; 'la chamba' = party; 'la lana' = sweater
'Hacerse pato' = apologize; 'la chamba' = garage; 'la lana' = paint
'Hacerse pato' = get angry; 'la chamba' = school; 'la lana' = debt
questions.explanation: In Mexican Spanish, 'hacerse pato' means to play dumb, 'la chamba' is work/job, and 'la lana' is money/cash!

dialogue.speaker: Álvaro
dialogue.spanish: ¡Corre, Elena, que el control de equipaje del AVE cierra en tres minutos!
dialogue.english: Run, Elena, the baggage check for the high-speed train closes in three minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.spanish: ¡Madre mía, qué agobio! Es que el autobús venía a tope por el atasco en la Castellana.
dialogue.english: Oh my goodness, how stressful! The bus was packed to the gills because of the traffic jam on La Castellana.

slang.actualMeaning: packed full / to the max (very common in Spain)
slang.example: El vagón del metro iba a tope a las ocho de la mañana.

dialogue.speaker: Álvaro
dialogue.spanish: Por los pelos, tía... Mira, somos el coche cuatro, asientos de ventanilla.
dialogue.english: By the skin of our teeth, girl... Look, we're car four, window seats.

slang.actualMeaning: by the skin of one's teeth / just barely in time
slang.example: Llegamos al embarque por los pelos.

dialogue.speaker: Elena
dialogue.spanish: ¡Qué alivio! En cuanto arranque el tren me echo una siesta hasta llegar a Valencia.
dialogue.english: What a relief! As soon as the train pulls out I'm taking a nap all the way to Valencia.

questions.question: Why were Álvaro and Elena almost late for their high-speed train ('el AVE')?
options: Their bus was packed and stuck in a traffic jam on La Castellana
Elena packed the wrong suitcase
They went to the wrong train station in Madrid
Their alarm clock didn't ring
questions.explanation: Elena says: 'el autobús venía a tope por el atasco en la Castellana.'

questions.question: Which train car and seats do they have, and what city are they traveling to?
options: Car 4, window seats, heading to Valencia
Car 1, aisle seats, heading to Barcelona
Car 7, dining car, heading to Seville
Car 2, window seats, heading to Toledo
questions.explanation: Álvaro says 'somos el coche cuatro, asientos de ventanilla' and Elena says she'll nap 'hasta llegar a Valencia.'

questions.question: How much time was left before baggage security closed when they arrived?
options: 3 minutes
15 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour
questions.explanation: Álvaro shouts: 'el control de equipaje del AVE cierra en tres minutos!'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Spain, what do 'venir a tope' and 'por los pelos' mean?
options: 'A tope' = packed full / to the max; 'por los pelos' = by the skin of our teeth / just barely
'A tope' = very slowly; 'por los pelos' = without luggage
'A tope' = empty; 'por los pelos' = with messy hair
'A tope' = broken down; 'por los pelos' = way too early
questions.explanation: 'A tope' means packed full / at maximum capacity, and 'por los pelos' means just barely / by a hair!

title: Mate y facturas en la costanera

dialogue.speaker: Micaela
dialogue.spanish: Che, Nico, ¡qué lindo solcito hay hoy en la costanera! ¿Trajiste el termo con agua caliente?
dialogue.english: Hey, Nico, what lovely sunshine on the waterfront today! Did you bring the thermos with hot water?

dialogue.speaker: Nico
dialogue.spanish: ¡Olvidate! Está a punto para cebar unos buenos mates. Y compré media docena de facturas con dulce de leche.
dialogue.english: You bet! It's at the perfect temperature to brew some good mates. And I bought half a dozen pastries with dulce de leche.

slang.actualMeaning: sweet bakery pastries (in Argentina, 'facturas' at a bakery are pastries!)
slang.example: Traje una docena de facturas para tomar el mate en la tarde.

dialogue.speaker: Micaela
dialogue.spanish: ¡Sos un genio! Sentémonos en ese banco frente al río que corre una brisa divina.
dialogue.english: You're a legend! Let's sit on that bench facing the river where there's a lovely breeze.

dialogue.speaker: Nico
dialogue.spanish: Dale, pero ojo con el primer mate que siempre sale un poco fuerte, ¿viste?
dialogue.english: Sure, just watch out for the first mate since it always comes out a bit strong, you know?

questions.question: Where are Micaela and Nico spending the afternoon?
options: On a bench facing the river along the waterfront ('la costanera')
Inside a shopping mall downtown
At Nico's office
On a long-distance bus
questions.explanation: They are at 'la costanera' (the waterfront) and sit on 'ese banco frente al río' (that bench facing the river).

questions.question: What did Nico bring along with his thermos of hot water?
options: Half a dozen pastries ('facturas') with dulce de leche
Two ham and cheese sandwiches
A bag of apples and oranges
A box of pizza
questions.explanation: Nico says: 'compré media docena de facturas con dulce de leche.'

questions.question: What does Nico warn Micaela about at the end?
options: The first mate always comes out a bit strong/bitter
The water in the thermos is already cold
The seagulls might steal their pastries
The park closes at five o'clock
questions.explanation: Nico warns: 'ojo con el primer mate que siempre sale un poco fuerte.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: When Nico says '¡Olvidate!' and 'compré media docena de facturas', what do '¡Olvidate!' and 'facturas' mean in Argentina?
options: '¡Olvidate!' = You bet / Of course!; 'facturas' = sweet bakery pastries
'¡Olvidate!' = I forgot it!; 'facturas' = electricity bills
'¡Olvidate!' = Never mind; 'facturas' = bus tickets
'¡Olvidate!' = Wait for me; 'facturas' = tea bags
questions.explanation: In Argentina, '¡Olvidate!' is an enthusiastic 'You bet / Of course!' (not 'I forgot!'), and 'facturas' are bakery pastries!

title: El recibo de la luz en la colonia Roma

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Lucía, no te pases... Acabo de ver el recibo de la luz de este bimestre y casi me da un infarto.
dialogue.english: Hey, Lucía, come on now... I just saw this two-month electricity bill and I almost had a heart attack.

slang.actualMeaning: come on / don't go too far / you're kidding me
slang.example: ¡No te pases, te comiste todo el pastel!

dialogue.speaker: Lucía
dialogue.spanish: Aguanta, Mateo, no te esponjes. Es que la semana pasada hizo un frío horrible y dejé el calentador eléctrico prendido un par de noches.
dialogue.english: Hold on, Mateo, don't get worked up. Last week it was freezing cold and I left the electric space heater on for a couple of nights.

slang.actualMeaning: don't get puffed up / don't get worked up or angry
slang.example: Tranquilo, no te esponjes, fue solo una broma.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.spanish: ¿Un par de noches? ¡Pero si subió al doble! Y tú sabes que ahorita ando bien bruja porque no me han pagado el proyecto de diseño.
dialogue.english: A couple of nights? It doubled! And you know I'm super broke right now because they haven't paid me for the design project yet.

slang.actualMeaning: completely broke / out of money (andar bruja)
slang.example: Fin de quincena y ya ando bien bruja.

dialogue.speaker: Lucía
dialogue.spanish: Tranquilo, mi primo Javi me debía una lana de los boletos del concierto y me acaba de transferir. Yo pongo el setenta por ciento del recibo.
dialogue.english: Relax, my cousin Javi owed me cash for the concert tickets and he just sent me a transfer. I'll cover seventy percent of the bill.

dialogue.speaker: Mateo
dialogue.spanish: Uf, qué alivio... Es que el casero ya me estaba moliendo por WhatsApp desde las ocho de la mañana.
dialogue.english: Phew, what a relief... The landlord was already nagging me on WhatsApp since eight in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Lucía
dialogue.spanish: Ya sé cómo se pone. Ándale, yo lo pago ahorita en la app y además te invito unos esquites si me echas la mano con las cajas de la bodega.
dialogue.english: I know how he gets. Come on, I'll pay it right now in the app and treat you to some corn cups too if you give me a hand with the storage room boxes.

slang.actualMeaning: lend a hand / help someone out (echar la mano)
slang.example: ¿Me echas la mano para subir este sillón?

questions.question: What caused the two-month electricity bill in Mateo and Lucía's apartment to double?
options: Lucía left the electric space heater on for a couple of freezing nights last week
Mateo left his computer running day and night
The landlord billed them for the whole building
Their refrigerator broke
questions.explanation: Lucía admits she left the electric space heater on ('dejé el calentador eléctrico prendido un par de noches').

questions.question: Why is Mateo broke right now, and how much of the bill does Lucía agree to cover?
options: He hasn't been paid for his design project yet; Lucía covers 70% of the bill
He bought concert tickets; Lucía covers 50% of the bill
He lost his wallet; Lucía covers 100% of the bill
He paid the water bill; Lucía covers 30% of the bill
questions.explanation: Mateo hasn't been paid for his design project yet, and Lucía covers 70% after her cousin Javi paid her back.

questions.question: What favor does Lucía ask of Mateo in exchange for treating him to 'esquites'?
options: Help her with the boxes in the storage room ('la bodega')
Walk her dog in the park
Call the landlord back
Wash the dishes after dinner
questions.explanation: Lucía says: 'te invito unos esquites si me echas la mano con las cajas de la bodega.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: What do 'no te esponjes', 'andar bruja', and 'echar la mano' mean in Mexican Spanish?
options: 'No te esponjes' = don't get worked up; 'andar bruja' = to be broke; 'echar la mano' = to lend a hand
'No te esponjes' = don't get wet; 'andar bruja' = to stay up late; 'echar la mano' = to wave goodbye
'No te esponjes' = don't eat too much; 'andar bruja' = to be angry; 'echar la mano' = to applaud
'No te esponjes' = don't fall asleep; 'andar bruja' = to be lucky; 'echar la mano' = to pay in cash
questions.explanation: 'No te esponjes' means don't get puffed up/angry, 'andar bruja' means to be broke, and 'echar la mano' means to lend a hand!

dialogue.speaker: Valentina
dialogue.spanish: ¡Aló, Pipe! ¿Dónde vienen? Llevamos media hora haciendo fila en la entrada del bar.
dialogue.english: Hello, Pipe! Where are you guys? We've been waiting in line at the bar entrance for half an hour.

dialogue.speaker: Pipe
dialogue.spanish: ¡Ay, qué pena con vos, Vale! Nos cogió un trancón horrible por la carrera Séptima.
dialogue.english: Oh, I'm so sorry, Vale! We got caught in a terrible traffic jam on Seventh Avenue.

slang.actualMeaning: a massive traffic jam / gridlock (Colombian Spanish)
slang.example: Salí temprano pero había un trancón monumental en la autopista.

dialogue.speaker: Valentina
dialogue.spanish: ¡No me digás! Bueno, apúrense que antes de las diez no cobran cover y la rumba está buenísima.
dialogue.english: Don't tell me that! Well, hurry up because before ten o'clock there's no cover charge and the party is awesome.

slang.actualMeaning: the party / night out dancing (standard in Colombia)
slang.example: Este viernes se armó la rumba en Chapinero.

dialogue.speaker: Pipe
dialogue.spanish: Ya nos bajamos del taxi a dos cuadras y vamos corriendo. ¡Guardanos puesto en la mesa!
dialogue.english: We just got out of the taxi two blocks away and we're running over. Save us a spot at the table!

questions.question: Why is Pipe running late to meet Valentina at the bar?
options: His taxi got stuck in a terrible traffic jam ('un trancón') on Seventh Avenue
He forgot his ID card at home
He went to the wrong neighborhood
His phone battery died
questions.explanation: Pipe says: 'Nos cogió un trancón horrible por la carrera Séptima.'

questions.question: Why is it important that Pipe arrive before 10:00 PM?
options: There is no cover charge before 10:00 PM
The kitchen closes at 10:00 PM
Valentina has to leave at 10:00 PM
Drinks are half-price until 10:00 PM
questions.explanation: Valentina says: 'antes de las diez no cobran cover y la rumba está buenísima.'

questions.question: What did Pipe and his friends do to get there faster?
options: They hopped out of the taxi two blocks away and are running the rest of the way
They rented electric scooters
They took the subway
They asked the driver to take a shortcut
questions.explanation: Pipe says: 'Ya nos bajamos del taxi a dos cuadras y vamos corriendo.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: In Colombia, what do '¡Qué pena con vos!', 'un trancón', and 'la rumba' mean?
options: '¡Qué pena!' = I'm so sorry / excuse me; 'un trancón' = a traffic jam; 'la rumba' = the party / night out
'¡Qué pena!' = How sad; 'un trancón' = a big drink; 'la rumba' = the band
'¡Qué pena!' = How embarrassing; 'un trancón' = a rainstorm; 'la rumba' = the street
'¡Qué pena!' = What a pity; 'un trancón' = a police checkpoint; 'la rumba' = the line
questions.explanation: In Colombia, '¡Qué pena (con vos/usted)!' is the polite way to say 'I'm so sorry / excuse me', 'un trancón' is a traffic jam, and 'la rumba' is a party/night out!

title: El boleto falso afuera del Foro Sol

dialogue.speaker: Paco
dialogue.spanish: ¡No mames, Mariana! El lector de códigos aquí en la puerta del Foro Sol acaba de prender en rojo con mi boleto, güey.
dialogue.english: No freaking way, Mariana! The barcode scanner right here at the Foro Sol gate just flashed red on my ticket, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Mariana
dialogue.spanish: ¡No me digas eso! Te advertí que ese revendedor de Facebook se veía súper chafa, Paco. ¡Se pasó de lanza el tipo si nos vendió uno clonado!
dialogue.english: Don't tell me that! I warned you that Facebook reseller looked super sketchy, Paco. That guy totally ripped us off if he sold us a cloned ticket!

slang.actualMeaning: sketchy, fake, or low-quality (Mexican slang)
slang.example: Compré unos audífonos baratos pero salieron bien chafas.

dialogue.speaker: Paco
dialogue.spanish: Espérate, ya me puse nervioso porque me costó un ojo de la cara y me quedé sin un quinto para toda la quincena.
dialogue.english: Wait a second, now I'm nervous because it cost me an arm and a leg and left me without a cent for the whole two-week pay period.

slang.actualMeaning: penniless / without a single cent left
slang.example: Después de pagar la renta me quedé sin un quinto.

dialogue.speaker: Mariana
dialogue.spanish: A ver, enséñame tu celular... ¡Ay, Paco, estás bien dormido! Estabas enseñando el código QR del estacionamiento en vez del boleto del concierto.
dialogue.english: Hold on, show me your phone... Oh, Paco, you're half asleep! You were showing the QR code for the parking lot instead of the concert ticket.

dialogue.speaker: Paco
dialogue.spanish: ¿Neta? ¡Qué oso hice con el de seguridad! Mira, ya escaneó el bueno y se puso en verde.
dialogue.english: For real? How embarrassing in front of the security guard! Look, he just scanned the right one and it turned green.

slang.actualMeaning: How embarrassing! / What a blunder!
slang.example: ¡Qué oso cuando me caí frente a toda la clase!

dialogue.speaker: Mariana
dialogue.spanish: ¡A huevo! Casi me da el patatús. Ya córrele que la banda está a punto de tocar la primera rola y nos toca hasta la pista.
dialogue.english: Hell yeah! I almost had a heart attack. Run now, the band is about to play their first song and our spot is all the way down on the floor.

slang.actualMeaning: song / music track (Mexican slang)
slang.example: Esa banda acaba de sacar una rola buenísima.

questions.question: Why do Paco and Mariana panic when they arrive at the entrance to the Foro Sol concert venue?
options: The ticket scanner flashes red on Paco's ticket, making them fear he bought a fake ticket
Paco forgot his cell phone in the parking lot
The concert was canceled due to rain
Mariana bought tickets for the wrong date
questions.explanation: The scanner flashes red ('acaba de prender en rojo'), making them fear the Facebook reseller sold Paco a cloned ticket.

questions.question: What silly mistake does Mariana discover when she looks at Paco's phone screen?
options: He was showing the QR code for the parking lot instead of the concert ticket
His screen brightness was turned all the way down
He was showing an old movie ticket
His phone battery had died
questions.explanation: Mariana sees he was showing 'el código QR del estacionamiento en vez del boleto del concierto.'

questions.question: Why do they have to run once the real ticket scans green?
options: The band is about to play their first song ('la primera rola') and their spot is down on the floor ('la pista')
The stadium gates are closing in one minute
It is starting to rain heavily
They need to meet their friends at the merchandise booth
questions.explanation: Mariana says: 'la banda está a punto de tocar la primera rola y nos toca hasta la pista.'

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: What do 'chafa', 'sin un quinto', '¡qué oso!', and 'la rola' mean in Mexican slang?
options: 'Chafa' = sketchy/low-quality; 'sin un quinto' = penniless; 'qué oso' = how embarrassing; 'la rola' = the song
'Chafa' = polite; 'sin un quinto' = five minutes late; 'qué oso' = how lucky; 'la rola' = the stage
'Chafa' = expensive; 'sin un quinto' = without a ticket; 'qué oso' = how scary; 'la rola' = the guitar
'Chafa' = famous; 'sin un quinto' = alone; 'qué oso' = how funny; 'la rola' = the exit
questions.explanation: In Mexico City slang, 'chafa' is sketchy/shoddy, 'sin un quinto' is penniless, '¡qué oso!' is 'how embarrassing!', and 'la rola' is the song!
